title: The Neolithic and Chalcolithic Levant
subtitle: 10,000–2,000 BC · Jericho, 'Ain Ghazal, and the Nahal Mishmar Hoard

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: From the first walled town to the giant statues of 'Ain Ghazal and Early Bronze urbanization

entries.label: Natufian Foragers and the Roots of Sedentism
entries.hint: Natufian communities in the Levantine hill country built durable stone-founded round houses and buried their dead within settlements they occupied for generations — evidence of genuine sedentism among hunter-gatherers who had not yet domesticated any plant or animal, a sequence that challenges any simple story of farming causing settled life rather than the reverse.
entries.note: Ain Mallaha (Eynan) excavations, Jean Perrot (1955–61 and later seasons).

entries.label: Jericho's Walled Town
entries.hint: Pre-Pottery Neolithic A Jericho built a massive stone wall and a freestanding stone tower over eight metres tall — among the earliest large-scale communal construction projects known anywhere, undertaken by a community with no writing, no metal tools and no draft animals, making Jericho a strong candidate for the world's oldest continuously inhabited town.
entries.note: Jericho excavations, Kathleen Kenyon (1952–58).

entries.label: 'Ain Ghazal and the PPNB Expansion
entries.hint: 'Ain Ghazal grew into one of the largest Pre-Pottery Neolithic B settlements in the entire Near East, its population estimated at several thousand at its height — a scale of Neolithic settlement that required correspondingly sophisticated arrangements for shared land, water and building space well before any recognisable state institution existed to manage them.
entries.note: 'Ain Ghazal excavations, Gary Rollefson and Alan Simmons (1982–89, 1993–96 seasons).

entries.label: The Ghassulian Chalcolithic
entries.hint: The Ghassulian culture of the Jordan Valley combined established Neolithic farming with the region's first regular use of copper, elaborate wall paintings, and distinctive churn-shaped pottery — a transitional horizon between the fully stone-tool Neolithic and the metal-using Bronze Age that gives the whole Chalcolithic period its name.
entries.note: Teleilat Ghassul excavations, various seasons from 1929 onward.

entries.label: Early Bronze Age Urbanization
entries.hint: Fortified towns with monumental gates, temples and planned street layouts appeared across the Levant during the Early Bronze Age at sites including Megiddo, Ai and a rebuilt Jericho — the region's first genuine urban settlements, still without writing of their own but increasingly linked into Egyptian and Mesopotamian trade networks.
entries.note: Megiddo excavations, University of Chicago Oriental Institute (1925–39) and later expeditions.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Evidence of violence and destruction across eight prehistoric millennia

entries.label: The Purpose of Jericho's Wall Debated
entries.hint: Whether Jericho's Pre-Pottery Neolithic A wall was built for defence against human attackers or as flood and erosion control against seasonal wadi flows remains genuinely disputed among archaeologists — a reminder that a structure's monumental scale does not by itself settle the question of what threat, if any, it was built to meet.
entries.note: Kathleen Kenyon's original defensive interpretation versus later flood-control counter-readings of the Jericho wall and tower.

entries.label: The Abandonment of 'Ain Ghazal
entries.hint: 'Ain Ghazal's population declined sharply and the settlement contracted around 6000 BC, a change archaeologists connect to environmental degradation from generations of overgrazing and deforestation around a site that had grown larger than its surrounding land could sustainably support.
entries.note: Gary Rollefson, on environmental degradation and the decline of 'Ain Ghazal.

entries.label: Early Bronze Age Destruction Layers
entries.hint: Many Early Bronze III Levantine towns show destruction or abandonment layers around 2300 BC, a period some researchers link to the wider '4.2-kiloyear event' climate downturn that also disrupted Old Kingdom Egypt and Akkadian Mesopotamia, though the precise local causes at individual Levantine sites remain debated case by case.
entries.note: Comparative Early Bronze III destruction-layer evidence across Levantine tell sites; debated linkage to the 4.2ka BP aridification event.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The first evidence of collective labour and storage control

entries.label: Collective Labour at Jericho
entries.hint: Building Jericho's wall and tower required coordinating the labour of a community numbering in the hundreds over an extended period without any evidence of centralised political authority — collective decision-making and shared labour obligation organised at a scale that predates, by millennia, the first identifiable rulers anywhere in the region.
entries.note: Kathleen Kenyon, Jericho excavations, on the scale of labour implied by the wall and tower construction.

entries.label: Storage and Surplus Control at 'Ain Ghazal
entries.hint: Substantial grain storage structures at 'Ain Ghazal point to some form of managed agricultural surplus and its distribution across a population too large for purely informal household-level arrangements — an early, still entirely non-state precursor to the storage-and-redistribution economies that later urban temples and palaces would formalise.
entries.note: 'Ain Ghazal excavations, Gary Rollefson and Alan Simmons, on storage facility evidence.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Plastered skulls, ancestor cult, and the Nahal Mishmar ritual hoard

entries.label: The Plastered Skulls of Jericho
entries.loc: Found: Jericho · Now: British Museum and Jordan Archaeological Museum
entries.hint: Pre-Pottery Neolithic B communities at Jericho and 'Ain Ghazal removed the skulls of certain dead, modelled facial features onto them in plaster, and inset shells for eyes before keeping or reburying them — one of the clearest surviving expressions of an ancestor cult anywhere in Neolithic archaeology, though which individuals received this treatment, and why, remains only partly understood.
entries.note: Plastered skulls from Jericho, British Museum and Jordan Archaeological Museum; Kathleen Kenyon excavations.

entries.label: The Nahal Mishmar Hoard
entries.loc: Found: Nahal Mishmar cave · Now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem
entries.hint: A cache of 429 copper, bronze, ivory and stone objects — ceremonial mace-heads, 'crowns' and standards of a sophistication far beyond ordinary Chalcolithic toolmaking — was found wrapped in a mat and hidden deep in a Judean Desert cave, almost certainly a temple treasury concealed during some crisis whose nature is not recorded in any surviving text.
entries.note: Nahal Mishmar Hoard, Israel Museum, Jerusalem; Pessah Bar-Adon, discovery and excavation (1961).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The lime-plaster statues of 'Ain Ghazal and Ghassulian wall paintings

entries.label: The Lime-Plaster Statues of 'Ain Ghazal
entries.loc: Found: 'Ain Ghazal · Now: Louvre, British Museum and Jordan Museum
entries.hint: Caches of human statues and busts built from lime plaster over bundled reed and cord armatures, standing up to a metre tall with bitumen-outlined eyes, are among the oldest large-scale human representations anywhere in the world — a technically sophisticated artistic tradition from communities that had no pottery yet and no writing for another four thousand years.
entries.note: 'Ain Ghazal statue caches, discovered 1983 and 1985; Louvre, British Museum, Jordan Museum, and Smithsonian collections.

entries.label: The Ghassulian Wall Paintings
entries.hint: Fragments of geometric and figural wall paintings recovered from mudbrick houses at Teleilat Ghassul — among the earliest surviving wall paintings from any Levantine site — used mineral pigments applied directly to plastered interior walls, evidence of decorated domestic space well before any monumental religious or palatial architecture existed to house comparable art.
entries.note: Teleilat Ghassul excavations, wall painting fragments, Pontifical Biblical Institute expeditions.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The earliest evidence of counting, sealing, and symbolic notation

entries.label: The Judean Desert Stone Masks
entries.loc: Found: Nahal Hemar cave · Now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem
entries.hint: A dry cave in the Judean Desert preserved a cluster of carved stone masks, among the oldest ritual masks known anywhere, alongside organic material — basketry, textile fragments, skull fragments coated with a black bituminous substance — that almost never survives from sites with normal preservation conditions, giving an unusually rich glimpse of Neolithic ritual material culture.
entries.note: Nahal Hemar cave excavations, Ofer Bar-Yosef and Tamar Alon (1983); Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

entries.label: Clay Tokens and Early Accounting
entries.hint: Small geometric clay tokens representing specific quantities of specific goods, part of the same broader Fertile Crescent counting tradition found from the Levant to Iran, appear at Jericho and other Levantine sites across the Neolithic and Chalcolithic — an accounting technology that let communities track agricultural surplus long before any script existed to record it in words.
entries.note: Denise Schmandt-Besserat, Before Writing: From Counting to Cuneiform (1992), on the Levantine token evidence.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Wild cereal harvesting, domestication, and the first copper metallurgy

entries.label: From Wild Harvesting to Cereal Cultivation
entries.hint: Natufian and early Neolithic sickle blades bearing the characteristic sheen of cutting cereal stalks document the Levant's central place in the Fertile Crescent's shift from harvesting wild wheat and barley to deliberate cultivation — one of only a handful of places in the world where plant domestication happened independently rather than spreading in from elsewhere.
entries.note: Comparative sickle-blade use-wear analysis from Levantine Natufian and PPNA sites.

entries.label: Chalcolithic Copper Production
entries.hint: Copper ore from the Faynan district in the southern Jordanian lowlands supplied the smelting operations behind objects like the Nahal Mishmar hoard — early industrial-scale metal production whose mining and smelting debris still visibly scars the Faynan landscape today, among the best-preserved ancient copper-production landscapes anywhere in the world.
entries.note: Faynan copper-mining archaeological survey, various seasons; comparative ore-sourcing analysis of Chalcolithic Levantine copper artefacts.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Plaster, pottery, and the Nahal Mishmar bronze-casting tradition

entries.label: Lime Plaster Production
entries.hint: Producing lime plaster at the scale seen in 'Ain Ghazal's statues, Jericho's plastered skulls, and Ghassulian wall paintings required burning limestone at high temperatures in purpose-built kilns — a technically demanding pyrotechnology that predates, and likely fed directly into, the later development of pottery firing.
entries.note: Comparative technical analysis of Neolithic Levantine lime-plaster production.

entries.label: Lost-Wax Bronze Casting at Nahal Mishmar
entries.loc: Found: Nahal Mishmar cave · Now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem
entries.hint: Technical analysis of the Nahal Mishmar hoard's intricately detailed mace-heads and standards shows they were cast using an early lost-wax technique, allowing far more complex three-dimensional forms than simple hammering or open-mould casting could achieve — metallurgical sophistication that took the wider Near East many further centuries to match at comparable scale.
entries.note: Metallurgical and casting-technique analysis of the Nahal Mishmar hoard, Israel Museum.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Obsidian and shell moving across the Neolithic and Chalcolithic Levant

entries.label: Anatolian Obsidian in the Levant
entries.hint: Obsidian tools at Levantine Neolithic sites can be sourced by trace-element analysis to volcanic outcrops in central and eastern Anatolia hundreds of kilometres to the north, part of the same long-distance exchange network structure documented across the wider Neolithic Near East from the Zagros to the Mediterranean coast.
entries.note: Trace-element sourcing studies of Levantine Neolithic obsidian assemblages.

entries.label: Marine Shell from Two Seas
entries.hint: Marine shell ornaments at inland Levantine sites like 'Ain Ghazal originate from both the Mediterranean coast and the Red Sea, showing exchange connections running in two directions across the region — evidence that Levantine Neolithic communities were embedded in overlapping coastal networks rather than isolated in the inland hill country where most excavated settlements are found.
entries.note: Comparative shell-sourcing studies of Levantine Neolithic and Chalcolithic ornament assemblages.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Climate amelioration and the rise of the first Levantine towns

entries.label: The Younger Dryas and the Push toward Farming
entries.hint: A sharp return to near-glacial cold and aridity across the Younger Dryas period put real pressure on the wild cereal stands Natufian foragers had come to depend on, a stress many archaeologists consider a direct contributing push toward deliberate cultivation once warmer, wetter Holocene conditions returned — climate as a plausible causal factor in the origins of farming, not merely its backdrop.
entries.note: Paleoclimate proxy evidence for the Younger Dryas in the southern Levant; comparative archaeobotanical evidence for Natufian dietary stress.

entries.label: The Rise of the First Levantine Towns
entries.hint: Early Bronze Age fortified towns at Megiddo, Ai and elsewhere established the settlement pattern — walled hilltop or tell sites controlling agricultural hinterlands — that would define Levantine political geography for the next two thousand years, directly anticipating the Canaanite city-state system of the following Bronze Age.
entries.note: Comparative Early Bronze Age Levantine urban settlement-pattern studies.
keywords: Rise of the First Levantine Towns

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Diet, health and burial practice across the transition to farming

entries.group: Health and Diet in the Farming Transition
entries.label: Skeletal Evidence of Dietary Change
entries.hint: Dental wear and pathology in skeletal remains from early Levantine farming communities show measurable change from the preceding Natufian foraging population's teeth — a physical, bodily record of the shift to a grain-centred diet that complements, and in some respects contradicts the assumed benefits of, the era's economic and settlement changes.
entries.note: Comparative bioarchaeological dental studies of Natufian versus early Neolithic Levantine populations.

entries.label: Emerging Status Differences in Burial
entries.hint: Chalcolithic burials at Ghassulian-culture sites show growing variation in grave goods and burial treatment between individuals, evidence that meaningful social and economic differentiation was becoming a normal feature of Levantine village life well before any of the region's Bronze Age city-states had a recognisable king or court to formalise such distinctions.
entries.note: Comparative Chalcolithic Levantine mortuary-variability studies.
